Aug. 2 (Asia Today) -- South Korea's National Assembly has passed legislation abolishing prosecutors' authority to conduct supplementary investigations, raising concerns about how flawed or deliberately obstructed police investigations can be corrected.

The revision to the Criminal Procedure Act passed Friday under the leadership of the ruling Democratic Party. Lawmakers from the opposition People Power Party did not participate in the vote.

The Cabinet is expected to approve the measure this week.

The amendment eliminates prosecutors' remaining direct investigative authority, including the power to conduct their own follow-up investigation after receiving a case from police.

Prosecutors will still be able to review police case files, decide whether to bring charges and request additional investigation from police.

The current Prosecutors' Office is scheduled to be replaced Oct. 2 by a Public Prosecution Office responsible for indictments and a Serious Crimes Investigation Agency responsible for investigations.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_98931" });

Supporters of the legislation say prosecutors' authority to request supplementary investigation will provide protection against incomplete or improper police work.

Legal experts, however, say the system may be ineffective when police investigators respond slowly, perform only minimal additional work or fail to address the central weaknesses identified by prosecutors.

Requests could be ignored or delayed

Under the legislation, the Public Prosecution Office could ask for an investigator to be removed or replaced when the investigator fails to carry out a supplementary investigation request.

Critics say that remedy would be difficult to use when an investigator does not explicitly refuse the request but instead responds passively or submits an inadequate investigation.

Replacing an investigator could also produce additional delays because the new investigator would need time to review the case from the beginning.

Park Kwang-min, an emeritus professor at Sungkyunkwan University Law School, said the authority to request a supplementary investigation was fundamentally different from the authority to conduct one.

"A request becomes meaningless if police fail to properly carry it out and simply allow the case to stall," Park said.

He said repeated requests followed by attempts to replace investigators could consume valuable time while evidence disappears, ultimately harming crime victims.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_14452" });

Kwak Dae-kyung, a professor in Dongguk University's Department of Police Administration, said prosecutors would be expected to evaluate investigations based largely on documents prepared after police had completed their work.

"Unless prosecutors fully understand how the investigation was conducted, it will be difficult to accurately understand the case from documents alone or provide specific instructions for further investigation," Kwak said.

He said investigators may know important facts or circumstances that do not appear in formal reports and cannot easily be identified by outside reviewers.

The proposed system could therefore depend too heavily on the conscience and professional ethics of individual police investigators, he said.

"Law is fundamentally intended to anticipate and restrain human selfishness and misconduct," Kwak said. "Creating a law with numerous ways to avoid responsibility reflects an insufficient understanding of both law and human behavior."

Murder investigation raises cover-up concerns

Critics have pointed to the investigation of Jang Yoon-gi, a 23-year-old man accused of abducting and killing a high school student in Gwangju, as an example of a case in which independent follow-up authority may be necessary.

Jang is accused of abducting Lee Chae-won, a student he did not know, in Gwangju on May 5 and killing her with a knife.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_88986" });

Police arrested him about 11 hours after the killing.

Jang reportedly claimed that the killing was not planned. Police initially referred the case to prosecutors without applying a sexual offense charge.

Subsequent reports alleged that Jang's father, a serving police officer, and officers involved in the investigation destroyed evidence or attempted to reduce the seriousness of the case.

A police investigation team leader was accused of removing cable ties found during a search of Jang's vehicle. The ties were considered potentially important evidence because they could have been used to restrain the victim.

Authorities have also investigated whether police officers used personal or professional connections to interfere with the investigation.

Park said cases involving alleged police participation in concealing or minimizing a crime would be particularly difficult to correct once prosecutors lose the authority to investigate independently.

"There would effectively be no way to prevent another case like the Jang Yoon-gi case," Park said.

He said prosecutors' supplementary investigation authority had provided at least a limited opportunity for an institution outside the police to identify and correct errors.

"Now even that safeguard has been removed," he said.

New serious crimes agency has limited jurisdiction

The Democratic Party has proposed creating a unit within the Serious Crimes Investigation Agency dedicated to supplementary investigations.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_62088" });

The agency is scheduled to begin operations Oct. 2 when the current Prosecutors' Office is dissolved.

Creating such a unit would require additional legislation.

The agency's jurisdiction would also be limited to six categories of serious offenses: corruption, economic crime, defense industry crime, narcotics, insurrection and foreign aggression and cybercrime.

It therefore could not conduct follow-up investigations into most ordinary crimes, including many murders, sexual offenses, assaults and fraud cases.

Critics say this could leave police with an effective investigative monopoly in cases outside the agency's limited jurisdiction.

They argue that removing the investigative function from one of the country's two principal law enforcement institutions weakens institutional checks and balances.

Critics question speed of overhaul

The legislation will fundamentally change a criminal justice system that has operated for more than 70 years.

Legal experts have criticized the ruling party for passing the measure without allowing enough time to prepare new procedures, revise subordinate regulations or fully consider concerns raised by lawyers and civic groups.

Park said the government should have created stronger mechanisms to supervise police before transferring most investigative authority to them.

"Lawmakers focused only on separating investigation and prosecution and ignored everything else," he said.

Park also questioned whether the new structure was consistent with the Constitution.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_67595" });

He said regulations governing special judicial police officers and numerous enforcement rules would need to be revised before the new system could operate properly.

Additional amendments would also be unavoidable, he said.

"The question of who will take responsibility for the harm that occurs during the transition is a separate problem," Park said.

Kwak said the overhaul could particularly harm victims who lack money, influence or public attention.

"Powerless crime victims will be left anxiously waiting without knowing when their cases will be resolved," he said.

He warned that prolonged delays and inadequate investigations could deepen public skepticism about the criminal justice system.

Supporters of the reform argue that South Korea's prosecution service accumulated excessive investigative and indictment powers for decades and needs to be reorganized to prevent political and institutional abuse.

The Democratic Party says separating investigation from prosecution will allow prosecutors to focus on reviewing cases and presenting them in court while independent investigative agencies gather evidence.

Critics do not necessarily oppose separating the two functions but argue that the legislation does not provide an effective remedy when police investigations are negligent, delayed or deliberately compromised.

The central issue is therefore not simply whether prosecutors should retain investigative power. It is whether crime victims will have access to an institution capable of independently correcting a failed police investigation.
